title: Execution Manufacturing System
promise: The line runs its own orders.

hero.h1: The line runs its own orders.
hero.dek: The execution system on the SCADA's own database: the plant model, the signed recipe, the calendar, the batches and the record — one database for the whole plant.

screen.caption: the plant tree, and the facts that fall out of it: the vessel, the machine the good count comes off, the counters

items.text: A machine joins the line and takes its place, in plant order, on every plan, every record and every report.
Mark one vessel with its capacity, its unit and the material it holds; the batch size follows from the vessel, nobody types a quantity.

items.lead: The last stage and its counter
items.text: Name the machine the good count comes off; every batch end and every yield figure is read there.
A material carries what it is, what one of it is, what is on hand against its minimum, and its density.
A powder bought by weight and dosed by volume; without the density the plan refuses rather than guesses.
Declare it made and name the line that makes it; the intermediate is modelled without a second catalogue and without a spreadsheet between them.
The catalogue shows what is short, and the shortfall is printed beside the order before it is planned.
A product carries its base unit, what one piece holds, and a ladder of package sizes, biggest first.
A machine with no counter reads not measured on the record; what cannot be known stays blank.

sections.title: The plant is described once.
cols: The execution system does not ask you to describe your plant again: it opens on the machines the SCADA already reads. You say which one sizes a batch, which one the good count comes off, and what each counter is counting, and the line reads its own shape back to you.
The batch size follows from the vessel. Nobody types a quantity.
A machine with no counter reads not measured on the record, never zero. What cannot be known stays blank, so nobody is asked to trust a figure the plant never made.
Without it the plan refuses rather than guesses — the density that lets weight and volume cross.

sections.title: Products, recipes, the quality door
The formula is signed before the plant may run it.

screen.caption: the quality door: draft, in review, approved, and the note kept with whichever was pressed

items.text: Says what goes in, on which machine, into which container and at what rate, and is frozen into every batch it makes.
A new version is written and sent to quality; approving the new one retires the old one in the same breath, and every batch keeps the copy it ran with.
Nobody may run an unsigned formula; the server refuses anyone but a supervisor, in its own words, and the note is kept beside the signature.
A draft is the only thing that can be edited and the only thing that can be deleted; everything else is kept.
Give the recipe its own name and its own timeline; both live on the line, and the order picks the one it needs.

items.lead: The container the recipe packs into
items.text: The batch size and the packing row are worked out from the container, and typed nowhere.
A recipe promising a rate the line cannot hold is refused, and the refusal names the machine that cannot keep up, before a single batch is planned.

items.lead: A setpoint bound in the recipe
items.text: Sent to the machine when the batch starts, on the same audited path an operator's own setpoint takes.

screens.caption: the recipe sheet: what each machine takes in and what comes out, grouped the way the product travels, and how big one batch is

sections.title: The formula is signed before the plant may run it.
cols: A recipe says what goes in, on which machine, into which container and at what rate, and it is frozen into every batch it makes. Nothing is edited in place after a supervisor signs it, so next month's improvement can never rewrite what happened last night.
Approving the new one retires the old one in the same breath, and every batch keeps the copy it ran with.
A draft is the only thing that can be edited, and the only thing that can be deleted. Everything else is kept.
The refusal names the machine that cannot keep up, before a single batch is planned.

sections.title: Orders, the calendar, the job
Nobody presses start.

screen.caption: orders on the calendar: each batch with its own expected window, laid one after another

items.text: Pick a day: one recipe, one number, one start time — the order, every batch, each batch's window and the line's own tags are minted in one press, laid one after another with the turnaround between them.
Declare a wash, a changeover or a shutdown on the day; the plan lays the batches around it and the availability number honours it instead of punishing it.
Name the signal that rings when a job begins and the one that rings when it is finished; a planned order starts and ends by itself, stamped with the plant's own clock.
When the line has not picked a job up, it says why before it offers anything; where it can, one press raises the line's own start signal.
When two planned orders could match the signal that just came, the line asks on the operator's own screen; the job starts at the signal's own moment.
An order can move or go while its batches are still planned; a plan that has already run is never rewritten, and the change is on the record.

items.lead: An order with no planned time
items.text: Can never be picked up, and the board says so rather than failing quietly.

sections.title: Nobody presses start.
cols: Orders live on a calendar, and minting one writes the order, every batch, each batch's own expected window and the line's own tags in a single press. Then two signals do the rest: the line opens its job when the plant says a job began, and closes it when the plant says it is done.
A planned order starts and ends by itself, stamped with the plant's own clock and not the moment somebody noticed.
An order with no planned time can never be picked up, and the board says so rather than failing quietly.
A plan that has already run is never rewritten, and the change is on the record. Nobody edits a record to make a job run.

sections.title: Batches and the boundary
Batches overlap, because lines do.

screen.caption: two batches running at once on one line: one draining at the packer, the next charging at the vessel

items.text: The engine opens the next batch at the vessel and closes the previous one at the last machine; two batches run at once on the board.
Declare a batch charged signal and a batch finished signal; every boundary is a pulse the plant raises, and any batch can come out short or over.
Leave those two signals alone: the vessel and the last machine's counters decide, and only the last batch of a job can come out short.
Park the two signals or declare them; the boundary changes hands within a minute, with no restart and nothing to reconfigure.
It goes to zero and keeps counting; the total before the reset carries forward.
A reading that is not good never judges and never counts, so a comms loss invents no boundary.
Each batch's made and used are read off the segments that tile the job, so the batches always add up to the job's own count.

cols: The filler is still draining one batch while the vessel charges the next, so the board shows both of them running. You choose who decides the boundary between them, and you can change your mind without stopping the line.
The boundary changes hands within a minute, with no restart and nothing to reconfigure.

sections.title: The batch record
Every number says who measured it.

items.lead: Every number says how it is known
items.text: Counted by a meter, declared by a person, or held by the arithmetic — on the same row as the figure.

items.lead: The yield card and its balance
items.text: The record's balance tells you when a meter is lying.
Sign the count: the signed number outranks the machine counter on every report covering that batch, and both stay on the record.

items.lead: Tolerance and time limit on the job
items.text: A batch outside either turns amber, shows its own arithmetic and asks one supervisor for one signature: accept as it is, hold, or reject.
There is no such button, and there never will be; a signed plan is immutable and a restatement is recorded where it happened, never re-planned.
The plan froze the material rows when the order was minted; each batch prints planned against used, material by material, marked on plan, off, or not measured.
Quantity is judged only when a batch is finished, and time while it runs.

sections.title: Every number says who measured it.
cols: The record's one habit is that no number appears without saying where it came from: a meter counted it, a person declared it, or the arithmetic is holding it. That is what turns a batch record from a printout into evidence.
The signed number outranks the machine counter on every report covering that batch, and both stay on the record.
Quantity is judged only when a batch is finished, and time while it runs, which is what keeps the board quiet on the forty batches that were fine.
A signed plan is immutable. A restatement is recorded where it happened, never re-planned. There is no such button, and there never will be.

sections.title: The jobs board and the phone
The board an operator can read from the aisle.

items.text: One card per job: ordered against made, the batches as chips, and the period's own tally.
Names the machine, the number it is heading for, what happens when it gets there, and the distance left.
It goes quiet on a boundary the plant declares by signal, because then the counter decides nothing.
The night shift stays one period across midnight, and a job carried in says which shift it started in.
Hold a batch, end it, or declare a loss on that batch's own row, so a move can never touch the wrong one under overlap.
Tap the card: the record opens in place — what moved every boundary, planned against actual per machine, planned against used per material, then the two signatures.
What is waiting for a verdict is listed, and it is signed from the same screen while the line runs.

sections.title: The certificate, from the engine
The certificate prints from the engine that prints the shift handover.

items.lead: A batch is a report window
items.text: The certificate exists the moment the batch closes, computed over exactly the thing that was made.
Blocks bound to the line's own signals: tiles with targets, period tables, trends with their limits, alarm journals, the batch blocks, consumption and cost.
On the server, in the plant's own clock: every shift, day, week or month — or every batch, every order, every maintenance job. Nobody presses anything.
Frozen on arrival, numbered, hashed. Run it again and you get a second document beside the first, never a refresh.
By name and capacity, proved with the signer's own password, bound to the hash, never edited and never withdrawn.
Printed on the plant's letterhead in three languages, e-mailed to the list, filed as a PDF, exported as a spreadsheet.
0 report servers · 0 third-party licences · 0 seats to read: every operator, supervisor, planner and auditor reads, prints, exports and signs.
The batch certificate, the shift handover, the maintenance record, the audit sheet for critical equipment, the excursion report, the monthly review.

sections.title: The certificate prints from the engine that prints the shift handover.
cols: A batch or an order is a report window, so the certificate exists the moment the batch closes. What the incumbents sell as a separate report server with its own designer, its own database and its own licence is an organ of the same platform, computing on the same rows the line wrote.
Page x of y on every sheet, an end marker, a document number, and a hash you can verify outside the building. A report that would print a blank certificate is refused while it is being designed.

A released maintenance job books a window the production calendar already plans around. The batch certificate prints from the engine that prints the shift handover. A reject count signed by the lab outranks the machine counter, and the period says it was restated. One security model reaches the sheet. Nothing to connect, because there is nothing to connect.

items.text: The module you have been reading is arithmetic over rows the SCADA already writes. Same pages, same alarms, same audited command path, same engineers' browser — and no store, server or connector between the plan and the line.
The line opens its job when the plant says a job began and closes it when the plant says it is done, stamped with the plant's own clock and not the moment somebody noticed.
The filler is still draining one batch while the vessel charges the next, so the board shows both of them running.

items.lead: Change who decides a boundary, while the line runs
items.text: Park the two signals or declare them and the boundary changes hands within a minute, with no restart and nothing to reconfigure. A system that lets you do that is not a system that was bolted on afterwards.

items.lead: Every number says who measured it
items.text: A meter counted it, a person declared it, or the arithmetic is holding it. That is what turns a batch record from a printout into evidence.

items.lead: The signed count outranks the machine
items.text: The lab's signed reject count outranks the machine counter on every report covering that batch, and both stay on the record.

A counter that ends your batches is bound in a recipe, a page, a trend, an alarm and a report block; before anyone re-addresses it, the Tag Lens shows every one of them. We know of no other platform that follows one tag through every module of the plant like this.
